# Ekarājajātaka (Ja 303)

**ID:** Ja 303
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ekarājajātaka* (Ja 303), translated as *The One King*, is a birth story in the third volume of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1883; Hazra 1994]. According to the commentary, the Buddha related the story while residing at Jetavana about a courtier in the service of the king of Kosala, referring back to the introductory circumstances of the *Seyyaṃsa-jātaka* [Fausböll 1883]. In the past story, the Bodhisatta was born as Ekarāja, the righteous king of Benares [Fausböll 1883; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. An expelled courtier, banished for misconduct in the royal harem, incited King Dabbasena of Kosala to wage war and invade Benares [Bareau; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. Ekarāja offered no resistance and was captured and hung upside down by his feet from a lintel [Bareau; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. Maintaining radiant loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward his captor, the Bodhisatta entered deep meditation; his bonds snapped and he sat suspended in mid-air [Bareau; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. Meanwhile, Dabbasena was seized by severe burning bodily pain; realizing Ekarāja's virtue, he freed him, asked for forgiveness, and returned the kingdom [Hazra 1994; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. The Master identified Dabbasena as Ānanda and King Ekarāja as himself [Fausböll 1883].

In Theravāda doctrinal literature, this jātaka is celebrated as a paramount illustration of the perfection of benevolence or loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī* / *maitrī*), as also presented in the canonical *Cariyāpiṭaka* [Bareau; Lakshmi Narasu 1907; Hazra 1994; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. With respect to text reuse, DharmaNexus detects Pali-internal sharing exclusively with the commentary *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (longest match §1.4–4.4), which embeds and explicates the verses opening with *Anuttare kāmagune samiddhe* [DharmaNexus; Fausböll 1883]. No cross-language textual alignments with score ≥10 are registered [DharmaNexus].

- [Lakshmi Narasu 1907] P. Lakshmi Narasu, The Essence of Buddhism (1907) — Cited the Ekarāja Jātaka as the quintessential illustration of maitrī/benevolence.
